TIP 1: State transit bid scoring changed after RFP close
CHANNEL: secure drop
RECEIVED: 04 May 2026

I am a contracts analyst in the North Cascades Transit Authority. I worked on RFP NCTA-24-118 for the Redline signal modernization package. The bids closed on 18 September 2024. The initial technical scores put Bowyer Rail Systems second and a lower-priced bidder, Ardent Signal, first.

On 23 September 2024 Deputy Procurement Director Elena Varga sent a revised scoring sheet that added a new "regional familiarity" category worth 18 points. That category had not appeared in the published RFP. The change moved Bowyer from 84.2 to 92.7 and moved Ardent from 88.9 to 86.1. The contract was awarded to Bowyer on 01 October 2024 for $7,840,000.

I have the original score workbook, the revised workbook, and Varga's email to the evaluation committee saying the adjustment was "necessary to keep implementation risk acceptable." Bowyer's account lead, Mason Reilly, had met privately with Varga at the Alder House restaurant two days before the revised sheet was circulated. The meeting appears on Varga's Outlook calendar as "Redline risk review."

This was not the only unusual handling around the Redline package. The procurement file normally includes signed conflict disclosures from every evaluator before scoring begins. In this file, Varga's disclosure was uploaded after the award recommendation, not before. The metadata on the PDF shows it was created on 30 September 2024, one day before the board packet went out. I flagged the missing disclosure to my supervisor, Helen Cho, on 24 September and was told by phone that "Elena has it covered."

I do not know whether Bowyer knew the score sheet would be changed. What I can document is that the published criteria were not the criteria used for the award, and the late-added category favored the bidder whose representative had just met privately with the official who ordered the change. I am willing to share the workbook versions, the calendar screenshot, and the procurement checklist if my identity can be protected.

TIP 10: Airline moved complainant instead of chief pilot
CHANNEL: encrypted email
RECEIVED: 29 April 2026

I am a flight attendant with Larkspur Air. I reported Chief Pilot Graham Voss to employee relations on 06 January 2026 after he sent repeated messages about my appearance and asked me to meet him alone during a Denver layover.

Employee relations manager Cora Lin acknowledged that two prior complaints about Voss existed. On 28 January 2026 I was reassigned from the Denver base to Phoenix "for scheduling stability." Voss remained on Denver pairings and was later assigned to train new-hire pilots.

I have the text messages, the employee-relations case number ER-2026-0142, and the base reassignment email. Another flight attendant, M., filed a complaint in October 2025 and is willing to speak if she can do so privately.

The reassignment created a real penalty for reporting. I lost my regular Denver childcare arrangement and had to commute for two weeks while trying to swap pairings. Employee relations described the move as temporary, but the scheduling system showed my base as Phoenix through the end of the summer bid period. Voss continued to appear on Denver training pairings, including the February recurrent training roster.

When I asked Cora Lin why the person who reported the conduct was moved, she said the company had to "separate working relationships without prejudging the matter." I asked whether Voss had been given any restriction on contacting me, and she did not answer. I am including these details because the company's response may discourage other employees from reporting even if the original messages are treated as a personnel issue.

TIP 2: Trial endpoint recoding before biologics submission
CHANNEL: encrypted email
RECEIVED: 07 May 2026

I work as a clinical data manager at Orison Immunology on the Phase III trial for nalderimab, our lupus nephritis biologic. In March 2026 the safety review group changed how "renal flare with hospitalization" events were coded in the integrated safety dataset used for the BLA.

There were nine events originally coded as serious renal adverse events. On 12 March 2026 Chief Medical Officer Dr. Lea Montez directed the data team to reclassify six of them as "disease progression not treatment emergent." The change lowered the serious adverse event rate in the treatment arm from 5.8% to 3.1%.

I have the Medidata audit trail, the 10 March safety review deck, and an email from regulatory counsel Gideon Park saying the original coding "creates a label conversation we do not want before filing." The altered dataset was exported as `ORIS-NAL-BLA-SAFETY-v4` on 18 March 2026.

The change was not made through the ordinary blinded medical review process. The event narratives had already been locked by the clinical safety physicians, and the case adjudication spreadsheet showed the original coding as of 06 March 2026. After Dr. Montez's instruction, the data-management team was told to enter the revised terms under a bulk query response rather than routing each case back to adjudication.

I raised this on a 15 March call with my manager, Sondra Ives, because the audit trail would show the same user account changing all six cases within a 22-minute window. Ives said the decision had been made above her and that the filing timeline could not move. I am not alleging the drug is unsafe on the basis of these cases alone. I am saying the submission dataset does not reflect the original safety coding.

TIP 3: HR closed repeated complaints against managing partner
CHANNEL: intake form
RECEIVED: 30 April 2026

I was an associate consultant at Kennerly Advisory from July 2023 until February 2026. I reported Managing Partner Owen Chastain to HR on 14 November 2025 after he made sexual comments to me during the firm's client dinner at the Tremont Club in Boston.

HR director Maribel Santos told me on 02 December 2025 that the matter had been "handled informally." Two weeks later Chastain was named head of the Northeast public-sector practice. In January 2026 another associate, Priya M., told me she had filed a similar complaint about Chastain after a September 2025 offsite in Providence.

I have my HR intake confirmation, screenshots of the Teams messages where Santos discouraged me from "creating a formal record," and the promotion announcement. I do not want Kennerly contacted until I have spoken with someone about protecting my identity.

The reason I believe this is a cover-up rather than a single mishandled complaint is that HR already had a pattern in front of it. During my November intake, Santos asked whether the incident was "another Tremont Club issue," even though I had not mentioned the location yet. She also told me that legal preferred "coaching and containment" because Chastain was leading two public-sector accounts worth more than $9 million in annual revenue.

After I resigned, I downloaded the firm's alumni packet and noticed the separation agreement included a non-disparagement clause broader than the version used when two male associates left the same month. I did not sign it. I can provide the unsigned agreement, the Teams screenshots, the HR intake number, and the names of two former associates who have described similar conduct to me.

TIP 4: County jail food contract steered to favored vendor
CHANNEL: encrypted email
RECEIVED: 01 May 2026

I am a budget specialist in the Marlow County Sheriff's Office. The 2025 jail food-service contract, solicitation MCSO-FS-25-04, should have gone to Northfield Institutional Foods. Northfield scored higher and was $610,000 cheaper over three years than the incumbent, Carver Dining Group.

After bids closed on 11 February 2025, Undersheriff Nolan Brix asked me to replace the cost-weighting sheet with a version that gave "transition continuity" 25 percent of the score. That category was not in the solicitation. The revised sheet pushed Carver ahead by 3.4 points.

I have the original procurement packet, the revised workbook saved under Brix's network account, and a text message from Carver lobbyist Tess Rowland thanking Brix for "keeping the kitchen stable." The county board approved the $5.2 million award on 03 March 2025.

The revised scoring also removed a finding from the site-visit notes that Carver had failed two surprise sanitation checks in 2024. The finding was present in the PDF I reviewed on 13 February and absent from the version attached to the board packet on 27 February. Northfield's lower price was described to the board as "not reliably comparable" because of transition risk, but the file contains no written transition analysis.

I raised a records-retention concern to County Counsel's office on 04 March after the award, because the procurement folder showed two different versions of the same evaluation memo with the same file name. Counsel's paralegal told me by email that the final packet was the only official record. I kept screenshots of the version history before access was restricted.

TIP 5: Night discharge from solvent recovery plant
CHANNEL: secure drop
RECEIVED: 05 May 2026

I worked the third shift at Meryn Solvent Recovery in Dayton from 2022 until I quit in January 2026. Beginning in late 2023, supervisors told us to bypass Tank 4B on weekend nights when the carbon filters were saturated.

The bypass line sends untreated rinse water into the storm drain behind Bay C. I personally opened the valve on 19 October 2024 and 16 November 2024 after shift supervisor Paul Henley told me to "keep the tote count clean." The water had a strong acetone smell and a visible sheen.

I have photos of the bypass hose, a copy of the September 2024 filter replacement log showing no replacement despite 312 operating hours, and the waste-hauler manifests showing lower pickups during the same period. The storm drain leads to Little Stillwater Creek.

The pattern was easiest to see during production surges. When the plant processed more than 18 totes in a shift, Tank 4B filled before the hauler's scheduled pickup. Instead of slowing the line, Henley or maintenance lead Chris Danner would connect the green hose from the service corridor to the floor drain behind Bay C. The hose was stored in a locked cabinet marked "winter salt line," which made no sense inside the solvent building.

I reported the smell once to environmental coordinator Mara Voss in December 2024. She told me the storm drain was "not my lane" and that weekend crews should not make written maintenance tickets unless equipment was damaged. I am not in a dispute with Meryn and left for a day-shift job elsewhere. I kept the photos because I worried someone would eventually get blamed without the records showing who ordered the bypass.

TIP 6: University lab retaliation after Title IX report
CHANNEL: intake form
RECEIVED: 03 May 2026

I was a postdoctoral researcher in Professor Daniel Kreel's neuroimaging lab at Merrow State University. I filed a Title IX report on 08 August 2025 after Kreel repeatedly made sexual comments during late-night scan sessions and touched my lower back while I was seated at the console.

The Title IX office interviewed me once, then did nothing visible for four months. On 17 December 2025 the department chair, Dr. Nisha Baer, told me my appointment would not be renewed because I was "not aligned with the lab culture." Kreel remained principal investigator on NIH grant R01-MH-77104.

I have the Title IX intake email, my calendar entry for the interview with investigator Celeste Nam, and Slack messages from two graduate students saying Kreel had acted similarly toward them. I can provide the messages if names are protected.

The retaliation was gradual before the non-renewal. In September 2025, I was removed from the abstract for the Society for Neuroscience submission even though I had run the preprocessing pipeline and drafted the methods section. In October, Kreel reassigned my scanner time to a first-year graduate student and told the lab manager I had become "difficult to schedule." The scanner calendar and manuscript revision history show these changes.

When I asked Title IX for a status update on 03 November, Nam replied that the office was "still assessing scope." No one interviewed the two graduate students whose names I provided. I am not asking anyone to decide the case from this email. I am asking that the university's handling be examined because the complaint appears to have sat idle while the person I reported kept control over my funding and appointment.

TIP 7: CRO excluded high-event trial sites from analysis
CHANNEL: encrypted email
RECEIVED: 08 May 2026

I am a biostatistician at Camden Ridge Research, the CRO handling a Phase III trial for Valmereon's migraine drug relutapant. In February 2026 our sponsor contact asked us to remove three trial sites from the safety analysis population before the FDA briefing package.

Sites 014, 022, and 031 had the highest rates of severe dizziness and syncope. The stated reason was "source-document reliability," but the query logs show the same data-quality issues existed at lower-event sites that remained in the dataset. Removing the three sites lowered the severe dizziness rate from 4.6% to 2.2%.

I have the SAS program change log, the 21 February 2026 email from Valmereon VP Clinical Operations Mara Saye, and the before-and-after table named `REL-SAF-ISS-Table-14-3`.

The exclusion was implemented by adding a site-level flag in the analysis dataset rather than documenting a protocol deviation for each patient. That matters because the clinical study report draft still describes the safety population as all randomized patients who received at least one dose. I asked the lead programmer, Teo March, whether the population definition would be updated, and he said the sponsor did not want "a footnote that invites questions."

The sites were not random outliers. Site 014 enrolled 42 patients, Site 022 enrolled 37, and Site 031 enrolled 31. Their adverse-event rates were high, but their missing-source-document rates were similar to Site 018 and Site 027, which stayed in the analysis. I can provide the query aging report, the SAS diff, and the email chain where the exclusion language was negotiated.

TIP 8: Defense subcontractor procurement steered through consulting fees
CHANNEL: secure drop
RECEIVED: 06 May 2026

I was a finance manager at Halden Avionics, a subcontractor on Air Force depot maintenance work. From 2023 through 2025, the Lakehurst sustainment office repeatedly structured task-order evaluations in ways that favored Halden after bid materials had already been submitted.

The pattern was regular. For task orders LH-23-441, LH-24-102, and LH-24-388, Lakehurst contracting officer Dana Mercer accepted "clarification" materials from Halden after the question deadline and allowed revised past-performance tables that other bidders did not get to submit. Within ten business days of each award, Controller Wes Loring approved a Graypoint Strategies invoice for 3.5% of the award value. Graypoint's principal, Cale Mercer, is Dana Mercer's brother-in-law. Across the three task orders, the Graypoint payments totaled $482,600.

I have the Graypoint invoices, ACH confirmations from PNC account ending 7721, and an internal email where Loring wrote, "Dana's channel has to be covered before the next option year." I left Halden in March 2026.

The invoices were vague and always used the same language: "strategic capture support and stakeholder mapping." Graypoint did not appear in the bid files as a subcontractor, consultant, or registered lobbyist. When I asked Loring for backup before approving the LH-24-388 payment, he told me to attach the award notice and not to "over-lawyer an established relationship." He also said the revised past-performance table was "how Lakehurst wants it scored."

I became more concerned when I saw that Graypoint's mailing address matched a townhouse owned by Cale Mercer and his spouse, who is Dana Mercer's sister. The relationship was discussed casually inside Halden but never disclosed in the Lakehurst procurement file as far as I could tell. I have not contacted the Air Force or Graypoint. I am providing this because the late evaluation changes, payment timing, and family connection should be reviewed by someone with access to both sides of the contracting records.

TIP 9: Dairy processor falsified wastewater readings
CHANNEL: postal mail transcribed
RECEIVED: 02 May 2026

I am a former quality technician at Fairbank Dairy Processing in Wexler County. The plant reports daily biochemical oxygen demand readings to the county wastewater authority. From April 2025 through January 2026, the readings submitted to the county did not match the meter values in our lab notebook.

Plant manager Roberta Keane instructed the quality team to enter capped values no higher than 290 mg/L because the permit threshold is 300 mg/L. The actual readings exceeded 420 mg/L on at least fourteen days, including 03 July 2025, 19 August 2025, and 04 November 2025.

I have photocopies of the lab notebook pages and screenshots from the county reporting portal. The discharge goes to the North Fork treatment system, which had odor complaints from nearby residents during the same summer.

The falsification process was informal but consistent. The lab instrument printed a daily strip with the actual reading, and the quality technician copied that value into the bound notebook. Before noon, Keane or assistant manager Dale Firth would review the page and tell us what number to enter in the county portal. On high days, the portal number was usually between 276 and 294 mg/L regardless of the instrument printout.

I kept copies for three months because I was the person whose login was used on several portal entries. On 05 December 2025 I asked Keane to enter the number herself if she wanted it changed. After that, my access to the county portal was removed, but I was still asked to run the instrument. The notebook, instrument strips, and portal screenshots can be matched by date.
